COVID-19 has gotten a lot of folks talking about "regular" flu and what it does. But what does it do? The US CDC publishes a lot of charts & data about "the flu." It takes a good understanding of math & statistics to really understand raw data; charts are much easier to understand. But the creator of a chart has many opportunities to intentional or accidentally mislead people who just look at the picture.

Let's look at what exactly, the CDC publishes about "the flu," and what exactly, those data and charts can teach us.

Glossary

First we need to lay out some definitions, to make sure we're all thinking about the same things.

Outpatient

"In the medical system but not in a hospital." Your local General Practitioner, an Urgent Care facility, or a local health clinic all provide "outpatient" care.

Pneumonia

Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the air sacs in one or both lungs. The air sacs may fill with fluid or pus (purulent material), causing cough with phlegm or pus, fever, chills, and difficulty breathing. A variety of organisms, including bacteria, viruses and fungi, can cause pneumonia.

-- https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/pneumonia/symptoms-causes/syc-20354204

Pneumonia is a generic term for "an infection that makes your lungs swell up."

Influenza

Influenza is a viral infection that attacks your respiratory system — your nose, throat and lungs.

-- https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/flu/symptoms-causes/syc-20351719

Influenza is a specific virus that attacks your lungs, among other things. The attack on your lungs can lead to pneumonia directly - or leave your body weakened so that some other pathogen can infect your lungs and give you pneumonia. (Or, maybe none of that happens and you don't get any pneumonia at all).

Pneumonia & Influenza (P&I)

Influenza is linked to pneumonia. In some data sets, the CDC will include Influenza & Pneumonia together as one thing. When it does this, it uses the term "Pneumonia and Influenza - P&I."

Influenza-Like Illness (ILI)

There is a lot of overlap between the symptoms of influenza and other respiratory diseases. Cough, sneezing, difficulty breathing, headache, fever, even pneumonia - can all be caused by "common cold" viruses, by other respiratory pathogens, by allergies, etc, etc.

In some datasets, the CDC will talk about the symptoms, rather than a positive lab result for a specific pathogen. When the CDC is talking about the symptoms, they use the term "Influenza-Like Illness (ILI)."

"Flu Season"

Influenza is seasonal - there are more infections in winter (in the northern hemisphere) than in other times of the year. The specific time where influenza infections are the worst varies from year-to-year. Because the beginning of the calendar year is in the middle of winter, looking at flu data from January 1 through December 31 might split the peak - and leave the previous year's peak in January, and this year's peak in December - leading to one "season" with 2 peaks, and the next "season" with none. This would make it hard to reason about the flu from year-to-year.

To compensate for this, the CDC starts tracking "flu season" in the 40th month of the year, through to the 39th month of the next year. This ensures that the peak of the real flu season lies somewhere in the middle of the data set, making it easier to reason about and compare flu seasons.

Preliminary Flu Season Estimates

The CDC maintains a webpage where they estimate the total "burden" of influenza here: https://www.cdc.gov/flu/about/burden/preliminary-in-season-estimates.htm

Here they estimate the total number of infections, doctor visits, hospitalizations, and the total number of deaths. Using these estimates, you can calculate the Infection Fatality Rate and Mortality Rate of this year's flu.

The actual recorded numbers of infections, doctor visits, hospitalizations, and deaths will be much lower than these estimates. The CDC publishes all that data on its Weekly Flu Surveillance page.

Weekly Flu Surveillance

The main webpage where the CDC publishes their flu data is here: https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/index.htm

They go into detail about the methodology behind their data here: https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/overview.htm

This is one reason I like using the CDC's data - while no dataset will ever be perfectly-accurate, the CDC at least tells you how they are getting their data so you can decide for yourself how accurate it may be, or identify the ways in which it may be in- accurate.

In addition to providing small charts of a certain visualization of the data, most of the sections also have a "View Full Screen" option that will bring up an interactive, high-resolution set of multiple charts of the data. This can be more informative than a single, small, static image embedded in the main page.

Let's look at what exactly, the CDC publishes about "the flu," and what exactly, those data and charts can teach us.

Weekly Flu Surveillance

The main webpage where the CDC publishes their flu data is here: https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/index.htm

They go into detail about the methodology behind their data here: https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/overview.htm

This is one reason I like using the CDC's data - while no dataset will ever be perfectly-accurate, the CDC at least tells you how they are getting their data so you can decide for yourself how accurate it may be, or identify the ways in which it may be in- accurate.

In addition to providing small charts of a certain visualization of the data, most of the sections also have a "View Full Screen" option that will bring up an interactive, high-resolution set of multiple charts of the data. This can be more informative than a single, small, static image embedded in the main page.

Virologic Surveillance

https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/#S1

This section deals with laboratory tests that confirmed the presence of influenza virus in a patient.

There are two sections, for two kinds of laboratories: Clinical Laboratories, which means "a lab run by the CDC," and Public Health Laboratories, which means "a lab not run by the CDC."

The CDC generates one chart of the data for you, which might look like this for "clinical laboratories:"

https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2019-2020/images/WHONPHL14_small.gif

Underneath, there is a link to "View Chart Data" which will show you the raw data used to generate the graph. You can use that data to generate your own graphs. Note: The link on the webpage updates to point to the most-recent numbers about once per week. The link included in this post will be out-of-date pretty soon!

What does it tell us?

The data shows how many tests were run, how many came back positive for influenza, and what types of influenza were detected.

  1. An increase in tests run suggests that flu season is picking up.
  2. An increase in % of tests that come back positive does suggest that flu season is picking up.
  3. An increase in % of positive tests claimed by any one type of influenza will show you which strain(s) are going around this season

The only reason that #2 above works is because the influenza virus itself is endemic to the US - meaning it's already spread everywhere - and because influenza testing is also widely available throughout the US.

If influenza were only in one part of the US, a high % of positive results might just mean that you were testing that part of the US - not that there was any signifiant increase in flu infections. Similarly, if testing isn't widely-available, you might completely miss influenza outbreaks in areas where you couldn't run tests.

Only because both the flu and flu tests are known to be spread more or less evenly across the US population, can we draw the conclusion that an increase in % positive tests means an increase in influenza infections.

Outpatient Illness Surveillance

https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/#S4

This simple little section tracks the non-hospital medical visits that are for Influenza-Like Illnesses (ILI).

The CDC shows a a chart of the percent of all "outpatient" visits - not absolute quantities:

https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2019-2020/images/ILI14_small.gif

If you click "View Chart Data" to view the dataset behind it, though, you'll find absolute numbers and can compute the percentages yourself. Note: The link on the webpage updates to point to the most-recent numbers about once per week. The link included in this post will be out-of-date pretty soon!

Why track outpatient visits for influenza-like illnesses? Why not just track outpatient visits for the actual flu?

Well, someone with a mild flu might visit their local clinic, get looked over and told "it's not serious; you'll be fine," then go home. They won't ever get tested and counted in the positive tests from the previous section. Someone with a new strain of flu that doesn't show up in the tests, also won't get counted. Or, it's possible that their local health provider doesn't have the ability to run a flu test on-site, and would have to send a sample off to somewhere else. Maybe the person just didn't want to or couldn't afford to pay for the test.

Looking at the % of outpatient visists that are for ILI can give insight into what the flu might actually be doing across all people, not just the ones that bother to get tested. However, the cost that comes with trying to get a picture of "the influenza cases that didn't get tested" is that you're going to include some people that didn't actually have the flu - they just had an influenza-like-illness.

Normally, you'd expect the % of ILI visits to be more-or-less proportional to the % of positive influenza tests.

What does it tell us?

  1. How common "some kind of respiratory ailment" is as a reason for people to go see their doctor this year.
  2. If the % is out-of-proportion with the % of positive influenza tests, that could suggest there is a non-influenza respiratory ailment going around.

Influenza-Associated Hospitalizations

https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/#S6

One step beyond the local doctor's office, we're now in the hospital. And since it's a hospital, it can run an influenza test so we're looking at actual confirmed influenza cases again. This time, though, the CDC's chart shows the cumulative - total - number of hospitalizations instead of the weekly rate. It also charts previous seasons in comparison to the current flu season:

https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2019-2020/images/EIPRates14_small.gif

Unlike the other charts on this page, they do not provide the source data for this chart.

This data also includes a chart on "select underlying medical conditions," which shows the % of hospital admissions who tested positive for influenza, that also had one of the selected other medical conditions.

A very grainy chart that's basically unreadable is embedded in the page. This is one of the situations where it's really beneficial to click the "View Full Screen" link - this brings up 3 new charts and does offer download links for the underlying datasets. It also breaks down influenza hospital admissions by various characteristics of the admittee, such as age, sex, whether they needed a ventilator, and whether they went on to die.

What does it tell us?

  1. The height of each line shows the demand each flu season put on the hospital system
  2. The week in which the lines start and stop growing show when flu season started and stopped in a year.
  3. The % of admissions with a specific underlying condition could suggest that influenza is made worse by that condition.
  4. The distribution of hospitalizations by age suggests which age groups are most at-risk.
  5. The % that required ventilators can be used to predict the total demand for ventilators for future flu seasons* (when combined with the CDC's estimate for a flu season's total hospitalizations)
  6. The % that went on to die suggest the survival rate of cases bad enough to require hospitalization.

P&I Mortality Surveillance

https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/#S2

The one everyone's been waiting for! This dataset shows the total number of deaths in the US by week, and how many of those were due each to influenza and to pneumonia. The CDC publishes a chart that shows the actual P&I (combined pneumonia & influenza) deaths as a % of total deaths, and two lines that show the "normal expected range" for that percentage.

If you see the actual number go outside those guidelines, you can easily see if there is a significantly-higher-than-normal amount of P&I deaths:

https://www.cdc.gov/flu/weekly/weeklyarchives2019-2020/images/NCHS14_small.gif

They also provide the underlying data, and as before, it is updated just about weekly.

Reporting Lag

There is a big "gotcha" here, though: the numbers get udpated weekly and they really go up by a lot, for as many as 15 weeks after they're first published.

Here are animations of the pneumonia deaths over time, and the total deaths over time, where each frame is graphed from a different week of CDC data. You can see that as time goes on, the numbers for each week increase significantly for 10 to 20 weeks after they are first published:

  • Pneumonia deaths
  • All deaths

As a result,

  1. Whenever you look at the data, expect to see a decrease in deaths for the past 10-15 weeks no matter when you look at the data and no matter what's actually happening.
  2. A decrease in deaths in the last 10-15 weeks does not suggest or imply anything about actual deaths in that period.
  3. An increase in deaths in any sequential weeks in the last 10-15 weeks suggests a significant excess mortality event - enough people died to make up for the reporting lag.

What does it tell us?

Remember: ignore the most-recent 15 weeks of data no matter when you look at the data!

  1. A significant increase in the % of influenza deaths suggests a more-deadly flu season.
  2. A significant increase in the % of pneumonia deaths without a proportional increase in influenza deaths suggests the arrival of a non-influenza respiratory ailment.
  3. Seeing a week-over-week increase in total number of deaths in any group of weeks from the most-recent 15 weeks strongly suggests a large amount of extra deaths beyond normal.
